what_it_does: When an AI model runs on specialized hardware, the numbers it works with can be stored in different formats — ordinary integers, floating-point decimals, or more exotic schemes — and each format trades off chip area, power consumption, and how accurately the model answers. This paper surveys an enormous space of over 35,000 hardware designs for the basic multiply-and-accumulate unit (the tiny circuit that does one multiply and one add, the core operation in AI math), spanning formats such as standard integers, standard floating-point, posit (a compact alternative to floating-point), logarithmic number system (which stores the exponent of a number rather than the number itself), and block-quantized variants (where a small group of numbers shares a single scale factor to save bits). Each design is measured for chip area, energy efficiency (how many trillion operations per second per watt), and numerical accuracy (how much rounding error the format introduces compared to full precision). The paper then identifies the 'Pareto frontier' — the set of designs where no other design is strictly better on all three metrics at once — giving chip designers a principled map of the best possible tradeoffs rather than requiring them to hand-search the space.
